transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, hi. Um… I guess what finally made me come in is that I keep getting up when I’m supposed to just stay seated. Like during client interviews—I’m a private investigator, so listening is kind of the whole job—and I’ll suddenly be standing or moving around, and then I realize the person noticed.

It’s not just work, either. I do tutoring sometimes, and even at book club, which should be easy, right? We’re just sitting there talking about a novel, and I’m up getting water or checking something or pacing a little. Anyway, people have started commenting that I can’t just sit and listen, and it’s getting embarrassing.

Thinking back, when did you first start noticing this restlessness and difficulty staying seated—was it something you struggled with even as a child, or did it start more recently, say in the past several months or years?

Oh, no, it definitely didn’t just start recently. I mean, I can make it sound like a “work stress” thing now, because my job is kind of… you know, waiting around and watching people and then suddenly needing to act, which is a weird combination. But honestly, this goes way back.

My grade-school report cards used to say stuff like I was bright, but I couldn’t stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother still laughs about it—she says I treated every classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. Which is funny now, sort of, but also… yeah, it was a thing even then.
Aside from the physical restlessness, do you also notice problems like losing focus on tasks, forgetting details, or your mind wandering when you're supposed to be concentrating?

Um… I’m not sure, honestly. The thing I’m most aware of is the restlessness, because other people can see it and they react to it. Like, standing up in the middle of something is hard to miss.

With focus or forgetting details… I don’t know how to separate that from normal life, if that makes sense. I mean, everybody’s mind wanders sometimes. Mine might, but I haven’t really been tracking it the way I notice the getting up and moving around. That’s the part that’s been bothering me enough to come in.
Do you often find it hard to stay focused on tasks or conversations to the point that you lose track of what was being said or done, even when you're not moving around?

I… I don’t know if I’d say “often,” because I’m not sure I notice it that way. Like, if I’m sitting still—which, honestly, is already kind of the challenge—then I’m usually trying so hard to look like I’m listening that I don’t always know what’s happening in my head.

Sometimes I’ll realize I’m thinking about, I don’t know, the lighting in the room or whether I parked somewhere I shouldn’t have, but then again that feels like something everyone does. And in my line of work you pick up random details, so it’s hard to tell what’s distraction and what’s just… noticing things.

So I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure. The losing-track part isn’t what I came in thinking about. It’s more that people see me moving around and then I feel self-conscious.

Aside from the restlessness, have you had ongoing problems with things like getting into conflicts, breaking rules, being defiant with authority figures, or acting aggressively toward others—either now or when you were younger?

I’m not sure. I mean, “conflicts” is a big word, right? In my work you run into tense people, and sometimes people don’t exactly appreciate being watched or asked questions, but that’s not really the same as… whatever you mean clinically.

As a kid, I don’t remember being, like, out to fight authority. I probably annoyed teachers because I couldn’t just sit there like a statue, but breaking rules or being aggressive—nothing stands out to me. My mother would probably have a whole more dramatic version, because she remembers every parent-teacher conference like it was a Supreme Court hearing, but… no, I don’t think that was the main issue.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others, blurting out answers or comments before someone finishes speaking, or having trouble waiting for your turn in conversations or lines?

Yeah… that one, yes. I do that more than I probably want to admit.

Like if I hear the younger detectives talking through a lead, I’ll just jump in with, “Did you check this?” or “No, ask it this way,” before anyone asked me. Or even with neighbors in the hallway—someone’s talking about something and I’m suddenly in the conversation with questions or advice, and then a second later I’m like, oh, I just barged into that.

It’s not usually meant to be rude. It’s more like the thought is already out of my mouth before I’ve checked whether it’s my turn to say it.
Do you often make careless mistakes or overlook details in your work, or have trouble organizing tasks and keeping track of things you need to do?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. In my work, details are kind of the whole job, so if I miss something, it’s not usually obvious right away—or I tell myself it’s because the situation was messy, or the client gave me half the information, which happens more than you’d think.

Organizing tasks… I mean, I have systems. Not pretty systems, but systems. Notes in different places, reminders, little scraps—actually I found a receipt yesterday with half a license plate written on it, and I spent ten minutes trying to remember if it was important or just from some guy who cut me off in traffic.

So… I don’t know if I’d call it careless mistakes exactly. I keep track of what I need to do somehow, but it may not look very organized from the outside.
Have you ever had a pattern of behaviors like lying, stealing, destroying property, or being physically cruel to people or animals, either now or when you were younger?

I don’t think so. I mean, lying is a funny one in my line of work—people lie to me constantly, and sometimes I’m not exactly announcing every thought in my head when I’m trying to get information, but that’s not the same as, you know, some lifelong pattern of lying to hurt people or get away with things.

Stealing, destroying property, cruelty—no, nothing like that comes to mind. I had a dog growing up, actually, a very stubborn little terrier, and if anything I was the one sneaking him extra food when I wasn’t supposed to. My mother used to say he listened better than I did, which was probably true.

But no, I don’t remember anything like being physically cruel or breaking things on purpose or stealing. That doesn’t sound like me.
Do you often forget appointments, misplace important items like keys or your phone, or forget to complete tasks you had planned to do, in your daily life outside of work?

I don’t know… outside of work, it’s harder to say because there isn’t the same structure. With work, there’s a file, a client, a reason I have to keep things in one place—or at least pretend they’re in one place.

At home, if I put something down, sometimes I’ll find it in a completely different spot than I expected, but then again I live alone, so there’s no one else to blame. Well, except my cat, and she does knock things off tables, but she’s not exactly hiding my phone with intent.

Appointments… I try to write them down. Whether I always remember where I wrote them is another matter. Sorry, that’s probably not a clean answer. I guess I’m not sure if it’s “often” or just normal life messiness.

Have you ever had distinct periods—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep than normal, or had racing thoughts, separate from how you feel most of the time?

I’m not sure. I mean, my energy goes up and down depending on what’s happening—if I’m chasing something on a case or waiting on somebody to call me back, I can get wired, but that feels more like the situation than some separate… episode.

Less sleep, sure, sometimes, but I don’t know that I’d say I suddenly don’t need it. It’s more like I stay up too late and then regret it, which is different, I think.

Racing thoughts… my thoughts are usually pretty busy anyway. Sorry, I’m not trying to dodge the question. I just don’t know if I’ve had a distinct several-day stretch that was really different from me. Nothing stands out like that.

Do you often avoid, put off, or feel reluctant to start tasks that require a lot of sustained mental effort—like writing up detailed reports or reading through long paperwork—because you find it hard to stay focused on them?

I’m not sure I’d call it avoiding, exactly. I mean, paperwork is nobody’s favorite part of the job, right? Detailed reports can sit there looking at me like they’re judging me, but sometimes that’s just because I know once I start I’m going to find three things I should’ve written down earlier.

Reading long paperwork… it depends what it is. If it’s interesting, or if there’s something in it I’m trying to catch, I can get through it. If it’s dry, legal-type language, my eyes start doing that thing where they move over the words but I’m not sure anything is actually going in. Though that may just be because whoever writes those forms hates humanity.

So… I don’t know. I probably put it off sometimes, but I couldn’t tell you if it’s “often” in the way you mean.
Do people often tell you that you seem to not be listening or that you drift off mentally when they’re speaking directly to you, even in moments when you’re not physically restless or moving around?

I’m not sure. People sometimes say my mind is somewhere else, but that could mean a lot of things, couldn’t it? In my line of work, half the time I’m listening to someone and also watching the door, or noticing what they didn’t say, or wondering why their story changed from Tuesday to Thursday.

But if you mean like… someone is talking right at me and I’m just gone? I don’t know that people tell me that often. My sister has said I get this look like I’m “three blocks away,” but she also says that when she’s telling me about neighborhood politics, and honestly there’s only so much one person can retain about parking disputes.

So… maybe sometimes, but I haven’t really noticed it as a big thing.

Would you say these patterns—being unable to sit still, interrupting others, or jumping in before your turn—cause noticeable problems for you in at least two different areas of your life, like both at work and in your personal relationships or home life?

Yeah… I think I have to say yes, even though I don’t love admitting that.

At work it’s starting to cost me. I’ve missed details in investigations because I jumped ahead or pushed too fast, and I’ve irritated clients—sometimes I can tell I’ve cut them off before they got to the part they thought mattered. And the junior detectives… some of them don’t want to debrief with me as much, I think, because they feel steamrolled. One of them actually used that word, which stuck with me.

Personal life… I mean, people close to me have their own opinions about how I come across, sure, but professionally is where it’s been hardest to brush off. I used to think it was just being sharp or efficient, but lately it’s more like I’m leaving dents.

Or even with neighbors in the hallway—someone’s talking about something and I’m suddenly in the conversation with questions or advice, and then a second later I’m like, oh, I just barged into that.

It’s not usually meant to be rude. It’s more like the thought is already out of my mouth before I’ve checked whether it’s my turn to say it.

inference.note: Confirmed childhood-onset hyperactivity-impulsivity (motor restlessness, interrupting, blurting) present since grade school with cross-situational impairment (work, tutoring, book club); inattentive symptoms remain uncertain/unconfirmed, so both predominantly hyperactive-impulsive and combined presentations remain possible. No evidence supports conduct/oppositional disorder.

doctor.intent: Assess presence of inattentive symptoms (e.g., careless mistakes, difficulty organizing tasks, forgetfulness) to distinguish combined presentation (F90.1) from purely hyperactive-impulsive presentation (F90.0)
doctor.question: Do you often make careless mistakes or overlook details in your work, or have trouble organizing tasks and keeping track of things you need to do?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about inattentive symptoms such as careless mistakes, overlooking details, disorganization, and keeping track of tasks, but the provided symptom profile only covers hyperactive/impulsive symptoms and general impairment, not this specific symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. In my work, details are kind of the whole job, so if I miss something, it’s not usually obvious right away—or I tell myself it’s because the situation was messy, or the client gave me half the information, which happens more than you’d think.

Organizing tasks… I mean, I have systems. Not pretty systems, but systems. Notes in different places, reminders, little scraps—actually I found a receipt yesterday with half a license plate written on it, and I spent ten minutes trying to remember if it was important or just from some guy who cut me off in traffic.

So… I don’t know if I’d call it careless mistakes exactly. I keep track of what I need to do somehow, but it may not look very organized from the outside.

inference.note: Patient endorses prominent hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (restlessness, interrupting, blurting comments) with childhood onset, but inattentive symptoms are less clear/uncertain rather than clearly absent, and organizational difficulties are ambiguous. Combined presentation (F90.2) added since both hyperactive-impulsive and possible inattentive traits are present, though not yet confirmed to meet full inattentive criteria.

doctor.intent: Assess for conduct disorder features (e.g., lying, stealing, destruction of property, cruelty) needed to distinguish hyperkinetic conduct disorder from simple ADHD
doctor.question: Have you ever had a pattern of behaviors like lying, stealing, destroying property, or being physically cruel to people or animals, either now or when you were younger?

target_item.reason: The question asks about conduct-disorder/antisocial behaviors such as lying, stealing, property destruction, or cruelty, which are not covered by the provided ADHD hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so. I mean, lying is a funny one in my line of work—people lie to me constantly, and sometimes I’m not exactly announcing every thought in my head when I’m trying to get information, but that’s not the same as, you know, some lifelong pattern of lying to hurt people or get away with things.

Stealing, destroying property, cruelty—no, nothing like that comes to mind. I had a dog growing up, actually, a very stubborn little terrier, and if anything I was the one sneaking him extra food when I wasn’t supposed to. My mother used to say he listened better than I did, which was probably true.

But no, I don’t remember anything like being physically cruel or breaking things on purpose or stealing. That doesn’t sound like me.

inference.note: Ruled out conduct disorder features (no lying, stealing, cruelty, property destruction, defiance) making F91.x less likely and not added; hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (motor restlessness, interrupting, blurting) confirmed and longstanding since childhood, while inattentive symptoms remain uncertain/unconfirmed, so combined, hyperactive, and inattentive presentations of ADHD remain possible pending further clarification.

doctor.intent: Assess for inattentive symptoms such as forgetfulness in daily activities, which would support combined presentation (F90.2) versus hyperactive-impulsive only (F90.1)
doctor.question: Do you often forget appointments, misplace important items like keys or your phone, or forget to complete tasks you had planned to do, in your daily life outside of work?

target_item.reason: The question is about forgetfulness, misplacing items, and failing to complete planned tasks, which are inattentive symptoms not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… outside of work, it’s harder to say because there isn’t the same structure. With work, there’s a file, a client, a reason I have to keep things in one place—or at least pretend they’re in one place.

At home, if I put something down, sometimes I’ll find it in a completely different spot than I expected, but then again I live alone, so there’s no one else to blame. Well, except my cat, and she does knock things off tables, but she’s not exactly hiding my phone with intent.

Appointments… I try to write them down. Whether I always remember where I wrote them is another matter. Sorry, that’s probably not a clean answer. I guess I’m not sure if it’s “often” or just normal life messiness.

doctor.intent: Screen for hypomanic/manic symptoms (elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts) that could explain restlessness and impulsivity as an alternative to ADHD
doctor.question: Have you ever had distinct periods—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep than normal, or had racing thoughts, separate from how you feel most of the time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about distinct episodes of elevated energy, decreased need for sleep, or racing thoughts suggestive of mania/hypomania, which is not covered by the provided ADHD hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, my energy goes up and down depending on what’s happening—if I’m chasing something on a case or waiting on somebody to call me back, I can get wired, but that feels more like the situation than some separate… episode.

Less sleep, sure, sometimes, but I don’t know that I’d say I suddenly don’t need it. It’s more like I stay up too late and then regret it, which is different, I think.

Racing thoughts… my thoughts are usually pretty busy anyway. Sorry, I’m not trying to dodge the question. I just don’t know if I’ve had a distinct several-day stretch that was really different from me. Nothing stands out like that.

inference.note: Childhood-onset hyperactivity/impulsivity (motor restlessness, interrupting, blurting) with less clear inattentive symptoms supports ADHD; combined presentation (F90.2) most likely given both hyperactive-impulsive and possible inattentive traits, but predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type (F90.1) remains possible if inattention criteria not met. Bipolar disorder and conduct disorder/ODD features ruled out based on no distinct mood episodes and no conduct/defiance history.

doctor.intent: Assess presence of inattentive symptoms (avoidance/difficulty with tasks requiring sustained mental effort) to help distinguish inattentive vs. hyperactive-impulsive vs. combined presentation
doctor.question: Do you often avoid, put off, or feel reluctant to start tasks that require a lot of sustained mental effort—like writing up detailed reports or reading through long paperwork—because you find it hard to stay focused on them?

target_item.reason: The question is about avoiding or feeling reluctant to start tasks requiring sustained mental effort due to difficulty staying focused, which is an inattentive symptom not covered by the provided hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it avoiding, exactly. I mean, paperwork is nobody’s favorite part of the job, right? Detailed reports can sit there looking at me like they’re judging me, but sometimes that’s just because I know once I start I’m going to find three things I should’ve written down earlier.

Reading long paperwork… it depends what it is. If it’s interesting, or if there’s something in it I’m trying to catch, I can get through it. If it’s dry, legal-type language, my eyes start doing that thing where they move over the words but I’m not sure anything is actually going in. Though that may just be because whoever writes those forms hates humanity.

So… I don’t know. I probably put it off sometimes, but I couldn’t tell you if it’s “often” in the way you mean.

inference.note: Patient shows clear childhood-onset hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (restlessness, interrupting, blurting out) that are prominent and consistently endorsed. Inattentive symptoms remain equivocal—patient repeatedly hedges, attributes lapses to job demands/external factors, and denies clear forgetfulness or careless mistakes—making pure inattentive presentation (F90.0) less likely. Combined type (F90.2) remains possible given some hints of organizational difficulty, but hyperactive-impulsive type (F90.1) is now the leading diagnosis. Conduct/ODD-type behaviors and manic episodes were explicitly ruled out.

doctor.intent: Assess for a core inattentive symptom (failing to listen/follow through when spoken to directly) independent of restlessness, to determine if inattentive criteria are sufficiently met to support combined type versus predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation
doctor.question: Do people often tell you that you seem to not be listening or that you drift off mentally when they’re speaking directly to you, even in moments when you’re not physically restless or moving around?

target_item.reason: The question is about seeming not to listen or mentally drifting off when spoken to, which is an inattentive symptom not covered by the provided hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. People sometimes say my mind is somewhere else, but that could mean a lot of things, couldn’t it? In my line of work, half the time I’m listening to someone and also watching the door, or noticing what they didn’t say, or wondering why their story changed from Tuesday to Thursday.

But if you mean like… someone is talking right at me and I’m just gone? I don’t know that people tell me that often. My sister has said I get this look like I’m “three blocks away,” but she also says that when she’s telling me about neighborhood politics, and honestly there’s only so much one person can retain about parking disputes.

So… maybe sometimes, but I haven’t really noticed it as a big thing.

inference.note: No evidence of conduct disorder features (lying, stealing, aggression, defiance) ruled out F90.1. Clear childhood-onset hyperactivity/impulsivity (restlessness, blurting out, interrupting) with some inattentive traits supports F90.0 (Disturbance of activity and attention) rather than hyperkinetic conduct disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (restlessness, interrupting) cause clinically significant impairment across multiple settings (work, home, social) rather than being confined to one context, which is needed to confirm criteria for ADHD diagnosis
doctor.question: Would you say these patterns—being unable to sit still, interrupting others, or jumping in before your turn—cause noticeable problems for you in at least two different areas of your life, like both at work and in your personal relationships or home life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It's starting to cost me professionally—I've missed details in investigations, irritated clients, and made junior detectives less willing to debrief with me because they feel steamrolled.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms cause noticeable problems across multiple life areas, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think I have to say yes, even though I don’t love admitting that.

At work it’s starting to cost me. I’ve missed details in investigations because I jumped ahead or pushed too fast, and I’ve irritated clients—sometimes I can tell I’ve cut them off before they got to the part they thought mattered. And the junior detectives… some of them don’t want to debrief with me as much, I think, because they feel steamrolled. One of them actually used that word, which stuck with me.

Personal life… I mean, people close to me have their own opinions about how I come across, sure, but professionally is where it’s been hardest to brush off. I used to think it was just being sharp or efficient, but lately it’s more like I’m leaving dents.

inference.note: Confirmed childhood-onset hyperactivity/impulsivity (interrupting, blurting, restlessness) with cross-situational impairment (work and personal relationships), ruling out conduct disorder/ODD features (no aggression, rule-breaking, or defiance) and manic episode (no distinct periods of elevated mood/decreased sleep need). Inattentive symptoms remain equivocal but hyperactive-impulsive presentation is clear and persistent since childhood, consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
